newsitem.title: USA: Dow hits 3rd straight record, dollar rallies.
newsitem.headline: Dow hits 3rd straight record, dollar rallies.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose to their third consecutive record Thursday as bullish investors quickly overcame a bout of profit-taking, but bonds edged lower ahead of next week's economic reports.

The dollar soared to a six-year high against the mark and a 3-1/2-year peak high vs. the Swiss franc after the German central bank signalled it was not overly concerned with the dollar's strength against the German currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 28.57 to a new high of 8,116.93, surpassing Wednesday's milestone of 8,088.38. Early in the day, the index had fallen about 90 points.
But in the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,450 to 1,367 on active volume of 571 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Standard & Poor's and the New York Stock Exchange composite indexes also climbed to new highs.
The session saw stocks succumb to profit-taking, only to rebound sharply in late trading as investors proved themselves willing to buy even on the slightest of dips.

"This has been a very powerful advance the likes of which is very infrequently seen," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "There are many things coming into focus that make this market different."

Those factors include large amounts of money flowing into mutual funds, strong corporate earnings growth, and remarks from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan to Congress this week that dispelled fears of an imminent interest rate increase.

The Fed, the nation's central bank, raised short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. Higher rates would also tend to slow the economy, hurting corporate profits and stock prices.

In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury edged down 2/32, or 62.5 cents on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.44 percent from 6.43 percent Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
With long-term bond rates near their lowest levels in more than seven months, investors were awaiting key economic data next week, especially the July jobs report due Aug. 1.
The dollar hit 1.84 marks, its highest since July 1991, before ending at 1.8345 marks, up from 1.8268 late Wednesday.
It also surged to its highest level against the Swiss franc since November 1993, reaching a peak of 1.5100 francs and ending at 1.5065, up from 1.4855 late Wednesday.
The dollar rose to 116.10 Japanese yen from 115.65 yen late Wednesday.

In commodities pits, pork belly prices soared on speculation that Japan was looking to buy supplies from the United States. July pork bellies rose the 3-cent limit to 85.80 cents a pound at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
September crude oil rose 14 cents to $19.77 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
August gold ended unchanged at $323.80 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,862.9, down 11.6 points, or 0.24 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-stock Nikkei average closed at 20,286.23, up 155.72 points, or 0.77 percent.
